problem: Imitation-learning VLN agents (DUET/ScaleVLN style) overfit to expert paths and generalize poorly to unseen environments. They also lack recovery behaviour once perturbed off the expert path. Prior RL for VLN uses step-wise sparse rewards and critics, which cause credit-assignment and instability problems.
motivation: Agents deployed in the real world face execution noise and early mistakes that push them into states never seen in expert demonstrations. The authors hypothesize that exposing the agent to diverse rollouts, both successes and failures, and learning from their relative quality gives a richer training signal than imitating expert paths.
key_idea: Fine-tune a pretrained VLN policy with critic-free, Dr.GRPO-style group-relative policy optimization, using trajectory-level goal and path-efficiency rewards, a step-level progress coefficient, and SFT replay on hard instructions.
insight: Comparing K sampled trajectories per instruction gives more informative signals than single-trajectory RL. Group-based RL (72.65 SPL) beats REINFORCE, A2C and PPO (70.68) on the same reward setup. Removing variance and length normalization (Dr.GRPO) beats standard GRPO (72.65 vs 71.23 SPL). The largest gain is robustness: under 3-step early perturbation SPL falls 9.99 for NavGRPO vs 22.20 for ScaleVLN. RL only, without SFT initialization, collapses to 59.82 SPL.
method: Group trajectory sampling: for each instruction, roll out K=8 stochastic trajectories from the current policy (batch B=8) and store old log-probs.
Debiased group-relative advantage: A_k = r_k - mean(r) with no std or length normalization (Dr.GRPO), broadcast to all timesteps; no value network.
PPO-style clipped objective (delta=0.2) with KL to the frozen pre-RL reference policy (beta=0.01), summed over timesteps without length normalization.
Trajectory reward: r = exp(-d^2/2eps^2)*I(d<eps) + alpha*(-max(L-L*,0)/L*), alpha=0.25, evaluating goal achievement and path efficiency.
Step-level progress coefficient: gamma_t = 1 + sign(A)*(d_{t-1}-d_t)/L* scales per-step advantage, so steps toward the goal get larger signal.
Hard case replay: instructions whose K rollouts all fail go into a buffer; when it reaches M=200, SFT on their expert trajectories is applied and the buffer is cleared.
Training pipeline: 30k-step supervised warm-up, then GRPO up to 200k steps at lr 1e-5; applied on top of DUET and ScaleVLN; results averaged over 3 seeds.

setting.backbone: DUET / ScaleVLN (topological graph vision-language transformer), RL-fine-tuned with GRPO
setting.training_data: Same data as baselines (R2R / REVERIE; ScaleVLN's augmented data for the ScaleVLN variant), with 30k-step SFT warm-up then GRPO up to 200k steps; no extra data
setting.observation: panoramic RGB views with topological graph map (R2R-CE via candidate waypoint predictor)
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints plus STOP (waypoint-predictor high-level actions for R2R-CE)
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT distances used only for training rewards)

numbers.extra: RL fine-tuning; avg over 3 seeds; OSR/SPL at 2 decimals from robustness table
numbers.evidence: Table main_results (R2R Val Unseen: 2.19/82/73); Table robustness (NavGRPO prob=0: OSR 89.18, SR 81.88, SPL 72.65)

numbers.extra: trained in discrete environments, transferred to continuous

numbers_note: Main tables print SR/SPL as integers for R2R/R2R-CE; the robustness table gives 2-decimal R2R val-unseen values.
results: On top of ScaleVLN, NavGRPO improves R2R val-unseen to SR 82 / SPL 73 (from 79/70) and REVERIE val-unseen SPL to 43.55 (from 41.84), beating GOAT and other baselines. Under 3-step early perturbation it degrades 9.99 SPL vs 22.20 for ScaleVLN, and it beats a HAMT-style value-based RL baseline (SPL 72.65 vs 66.12).
limitations: Inherits base-model failures: group-relative optimization may amplify systematic errors when all rollouts share the same mistake.
Training cost grows with K (86 vs 46 min/1k steps, 28.7 GB peak memory at K=8).
Fails on ambiguous compositional spatial references, e.g. 'second bedroom to your left'.
